slides.title: Compact Homogeneous Kahler Manifolds
slides.notes: Open by placing the chapter after the homogeneous Riemannian material: the symmetry group is still the organizing object, but the complex structure now becomes equally decisive. The compact homogeneous Kahler case is unusually teachable because many analytic-looking quantities reduce to invariant algebra on a Lie algebra. Stress that the deck follows constructions rather than a taxonomy of examples: orbit, complex structure, symplectic form, metric, Ricci form, and finally the Einstein test.

slides.title: The Reading Problem
slides.notes: Use this slide to keep the lecture from becoming a list of Lie-theoretic definitions. The central move is that homogeneity lets us compute at a base point, while the Kahler condition forces the curvature form to carry complex type and cohomological meaning. Compactness is not a decorative hypothesis; it is what makes positivity, integration, and Chern-class constraints part of the story. Students should leave the slide with a question they can test on every example.

slides.title: Adjoint Orbits As Manifolds
slides.notes: Develop the orbit picture before mentioning flags. A point in the Lie algebra moves under conjugation, and the tangent directions at that point are bracket directions. This makes adjoint orbits ideal homogeneous spaces: the stabilizer is visible, the tangent space has a quotient description, and invariant tensors can be described by their values at one point. The slide prepares the later formulas for symplectic and complex structures.

slides.title: Roots Split The Tangent Space
slides.notes: The algebraic point of the slide is that the tangent space is not an undifferentiated vector space. It arrives decomposed into root blocks, and those blocks are the natural coordinates for invariant metrics and forms. A positive-root choice is more than notation; it fixes which half of the complexified tangent space is treated as holomorphic. This is the first place where representation theory begins to encode complex geometry.

slides.title: Canonical Complex Structures
slides.notes: Connect the abstract tensor J to a rule students can inspect on root spaces. On each real root plane, J is a quarter-turn, but the global issue is whether these choices are compatible with brackets. The positive-root convention provides that compatibility for the canonical structures used in the chapter. Emphasize that the construction is invariant, so defining it at the base point defines it everywhere.

slides.title: The KKS Form Is The Orbit Area Form
slides.notes: This is the symplectic heart of the chapter. The formula is compact, but it hides a great deal: tangent vectors are represented by brackets, the pairing uses an invariant inner product, and the result is independent of representative choices. Present the green region as the infinitesimal area measured by the orbit itself rather than by an external coordinate chart. The closedness of the form is what lets the orbit enter Kahler geometry rather than merely almost-Hermitian geometry.

slides.title: Compatibility Produces Kahler Metrics
slides.notes: Make the triangle of structures explicit. In general Kahler geometry one often starts with a metric and obtains a form, but on homogeneous orbits it is natural to build the form and complex structure first. Positivity is the remaining condition that converts the construction into a Riemannian metric. This slide is also the place to foreshadow that different root weights produce different invariant Kahler metrics on the same complex manifold.

slides.title: Invariant Metrics Are Weighted Root Blocks
slides.notes: Students often need permission to think of invariant metrics as finite-dimensional data. The slide gives that permission: the continuous tensor field is determined by a handful of positive numbers once the homogeneous decomposition is fixed. This is not merely computational convenience; it is why compact homogeneous Kahler-Einstein examples can be studied by algebraic equations. Keep the phrase positive weights in view because it will matter for both Kahler classes and Einstein normalization.

slides.title: Ricci Form: Curvature With Cohomology Memory
slides.notes: This slide should slow down the transition from metric curvature to topology. In Kahler geometry the Ricci tensor can be encoded as the Ricci form, and that form has a cohomology class determined by the first Chern class. The Einstein equation therefore cannot be separated from the Kahler class. On homogeneous spaces the representative can often be written invariantly, but its class is still the controlling memory of the complex structure.

slides.title: The Einstein Test In A Kahler Class
slides.notes: The purpose here is to make the Einstein equation look finite-dimensional without making it look trivial. Because all relevant forms are invariant, one compares their coefficients on the same root-block basis. The proportionality constant is not arbitrary bookkeeping: it reflects the sign and scale of the first Chern class relative to the Kahler class. For compact homogeneous Kahler manifolds, this is why the algebraic matching problem can produce canonical examples.

slides.title: Flag Manifolds As Running Examples
slides.notes: Use examples as calibration devices rather than as a detour. The projective line is the simplest orbit where the symplectic, complex, and metric pictures can all be seen at once. Complex projective space shows how isotropy irreducibility collapses the metric parameters. The full flag manifold in three dimensions is the first classroom-friendly case where several root blocks make the Einstein coefficient comparison visibly nontrivial.

slides.title: Moment-Polytope Intuition
slides.notes: This visual gives students a second way to remember adjoint and coadjoint orbits. The torus action compresses part of the symplectic geometry into a convex polytope, whose vertices come from the Weyl group orbit. Avoid overclaiming: the polytope does not contain all curvature information. Its lecture value is that it makes positivity cones, root directions, and symmetry visible in one picture.

slides.title: Proof Roadmap: Why Homogeneity Helps
slides.notes: This is a proof-architecture slide, not a theorem statement. The idea is to show where each hypothesis is used: homogeneity gives the reduction, compact Lie theory gives the root decomposition, Kahler geometry gives closed positive forms, and curvature computation gives the Ricci comparison. If students get lost in formulas later, send them back to these four verbs. They form the mental checklist for reading the chapter.

slides.title: Invariant Ricci Forms Are Algebraic
slides.notes: This slide explains why the chapter can discuss Ricci curvature without writing a local coordinate curvature computation on every page. Homogeneity moves the computation to the base point, while the bracket structure tells us how invariant vector fields interact. The metric weights still matter, so the result is not purely topological. The output is algebraic enough to compare with the Kahler form block by block.

slides.title: Cohomology Fixes The Target Class
slides.notes: The class picture prevents a common overemphasis on local curvature formulas. In Kahler geometry the Ricci form remembers the first Chern class, so changing the metric changes the representative but not the cohomology class. The Kahler form, by contrast, records the selected Kahler class. The Einstein equation can therefore be read as an alignment statement inside cohomology before any pointwise coefficient comparison is attempted.

slides.title: Common Misreadings
slides.notes: Pause here before the final exercise and synthesis. These misconceptions are natural because each construction looks canonical once it has been built. The correction is that compatibility conditions are doing the mathematical labor: brackets for integrability, positivity for the metric, and Chern-class information for Ricci curvature. This slide is a useful diagnostic for whether students are following the dependencies rather than memorizing names.

slides.title: Exercise: The Three-Block Flag Test
slides.notes: This exercise is deliberately qualitative so that it works at the board without a long computation. The key answer is not a numerical value; it is the list of data required to compare the forms. Students should name the tangent summands, the complex orientation, the Kahler coefficients, and the Ricci coefficients. If they can explain why equal ratios matter, they understand the finite-dimensional reduction of the Einstein equation.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the construction pipeline from the title slide. The chapter is powerful because it turns difficult geometric existence questions into invariant algebra while preserving the Kahler meaning of curvature. The orbit supplies the space, roots supply the complex directions, the KKS form supplies the symplectic class, and the Ricci form supplies the Einstein test. The next natural comparison is with later Kahler-Einstein existence results, where homogeneity is no longer available to do so much of the work.
